567	We disclose a bug discovered during development that affected intermediate results for QwQ-32B.
568	
569	\paragraph{Issue.} In experiment M002 (text baseline evaluation), the QwQ-32B text probe was inadvertently initialized with a midpoint heuristic placeholder rather than true sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Specifically, the placeholder assigned each step a feature vector equal to the midpoint between the mean safe and mean unsafe embeddings from the training set, with small Gaussian noise added. This made the text probe trivially predictive and produced a spuriously significant result ($p{=}0.001$ for HS vs. text FPR difference).
570	
571	\paragraph{Discovery and correction.} The bug was identified during a systematic audit of the feature extraction pipeline. After correction (using actual sentence embeddings), the QwQ-32B and R1-32B modality comparisons at the originally selected layers (L2 and L10, chosen by the biased composite metric) showed no significant HS advantage: QwQ-32B accuracy $p{=}0.828$, precision $p{=}0.346$; R1-32B precision $p{=}0.050$ but no tests surviving Holm-Bonferroni. The subsequent discovery that these layer selections were themselves artifacts of metric bias (\cref{sec:layer-results}) led to the corrected-layer analysis reported in the main text, where all four models show significant HS advantage$^\dagger$ at corrected deep layers, from strong (OT-7B) to qualified (R1-32B) (\cref{tab:hs_vs_text}).
572	
573	\paragraph{Impact on reported results.} All numbers reported in this paper use the corrected text embedding pipeline. The bug affected only QwQ-32B text probe features. The correction, combined with the separate layer selection correction (\cref{sec:layer-results}), means that early-stage intermediate results (non-significant 32B modality comparisons) reflected two compounding errors: incorrect text features and biased layer selection. Both are fully resolved in the final analysis.
574	
575	\paragraph{Commitment to transparency.} We report this bug to maintain scientific integrity. Code and data will be released upon publication.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1~\cite{deepseekr1} and QwQ~\cite{qwq} scale inference-time computation through extended chains of thought (CoT). Recent work documents that these models can ``self-jailbreak'': without adversarial input modification, the CoT transitions from safety-aware deliberation to committed harmful generation~\cite{harmthoughts,selfjailbreak}. We define the first reasoning step after which safety deliberation permanently ceases as the \textbf{Safety Commitment Point} (CP). This failure mode differs qualitatively from adversarial jailbreaks on standard LLMs because the harmful transition originates within the model's own reasoning. Before building production detectors, a prior question must be answered: can current probing methods reliably distinguish pre-CP from post-CP reasoning steps, and under what conditions? This paper provides a systematic characterization of what hidden-state and text-based probes can and cannot detect.

Existing safety detectors target fundamentally different problems. Hidden-state (HS) methods such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} classify adversarial inputs at the token level, while text monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} scan generated reasoning for explicit violations. Neither tracks the gradual, multi-step commitment process. A practical question is whether a monitoring system should read the model's hidden states or its generated text, but the reliability of HS safety probes depends on methodological choices that have not been systematically examined. Chief among these is layer selection: HS probes require choosing which transformer layer to monitor, a researcher degree of freedom whose metric sensitivity has received almost no scrutiny. We show it can reverse a study's central conclusion.

We present the first systematic evaluation across four reasoning models spanning two architectures (Llama, Qwen) and two scales (7--8B, 32B). Our central finding is methodological: the choice of layer selection metric entirely determines whether an HS advantage is observed. A composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) selects shallow layers for 32B models because shallow representations compress directional information, so a linear probe operates near the noise floor and threshold crossings reflect noise rather than semantic transitions. At these layers, only the two 7--8B models show significant HS advantage.

Threshold-dependent metrics excluding crossing rate consistently select deep layers (\cref{tab:layer_selection}), where three of four models show confirmed HS advantage (precision +19.2 to +21.9pp, Holm-Bonferroni corrected; \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}). R1-32B$^\dagger$ passes HB (+15.4pp) but its advantage is position-mediated (residualized gap NS; \cref{sec:experiments}); QwQ-32B$^\dagger$'s position baseline is competitive in balanced accuracy (\cref{sec:32b-analysis}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Layer selection sensitivity.} We identify a systematic bias in composite metrics that reverses HS probe conclusions at 32B scale. A five-metric ablation establishes principled selection criteria (\cref{sec:layer-results}).

    \item \textbf{Encoder-quality boundary with evidence gradient.} The HS advantage is significant against 384d MiniLM in three of four models (+19.2 to +21.9pp, HB corrected); R1-32B$^\dagger$ passes HB (+15.4pp) but its advantage is position-mediated. Against 1024d BGE-large, only OT-7B survives correction (1/4 HB). PCA capacity matching preserves significance. Evidence ranges from confirmed (OT-7B, R1-8B) to exploratory (R1-32B$^\dagger$; \cref{sec:32b-analysis}).

    \item \textbf{Negative results define method boundaries.} No alternative method consistently matches supervised probing at any evidence tier (\cref{tab:negative}): BOCPD/CUSUM fail on gradual transitions; Mahalanobis distance finds near-zero separation; RepE shows inconsistent performance across models (competitive on QwQ-32B, poor elsewhere); cross-model transfer fails under PCA alignment. Control task selectivity (11.1--16.8pp above chance; \cref{app:control}) confirms genuine safety structure.
\end{itemize}

\noindent These findings establish the observational foundation for hidden-state safety monitoring and identify layer selection as a critical confound that future work must address.

content.content: 1:Reasoning models with chain-of-thought (CoT) can self-jailbreak: their reasoning traces transition from safe deliberation to committed harmful generation without adversarial input. Detecting the commitment point (CP), the reasoning step after which a model's chain of thought becomes irreversibly committed to an unsafe conclusion, requires monitoring internal representations or generated text. We study four reasoning LLMs on the HarmThoughts safety-probing benchmark and show that the outcome of this comparison depends critically on which transformer layer is monitored. A crossing-rate composite metric masks the hidden-state (HS) advantage at 32B scale by selecting shallow layers where representation compression inflates threshold crossings. Threshold-based layer selection recovers significant HS precision gains in three of four models (+19.2 to +21.9pp, Holm-Bonferroni corrected); the fourth model's (R1-32B) advantage is position-mediated (residualized gap below minimum detectable effect). Encoder quality bounds the advantage: against a stronger 1024-dimensional text encoder, only 1/4 models survives correction. Layer selection sensitivity is the robust methodological finding; the empirical HS advantage is conditional, and current probes characterize the commitment phenomenon rather than constitute production detectors.

lines: \subsection{Layer Selection Sensitivity}
\label{sec:layer-sensitivity}

-Layer selection is a researcher degree of freedom that can reverse modality comparison conclusions. We evaluate five metrics: balanced accuracy (BA), precision, and inverse FPR are standard probing metrics~\citep{belinkov2022probing}; crossing rate and additive composite come from the safety detection literature. A multiplicative composite (BA $\times$ crossing rate) serves as the \emph{crossing-rate composite} (CR-composite) baseline, so named because it incorporates crossing rate in the selection criterion. Metrics evaluating probe performance at a fixed decision threshold (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) form the \emph{threshold-based} selection. This classification is an empirical observation from metric disagreement, not an a priori design choice; the ablation in \cref{tab:layer_selection} is a reproducible empirical fact independent of our framing. Crossing rate inflates at shallow layers where representations are compressed (inter-step cosine distances 1.4--2.7$\times$ smaller; \cref{app:cosine_volatility}), so threshold crossings reflect noise rather than signal. While BA, precision, and FPR share a confusion matrix with 2 degrees of freedom, the ablation diagnoses which \emph{aspect} drives layer selection bias. \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1~\cite{deepseekr1} and QwQ~\cite{qwq} scale inference-time computation through extended chains of thought (CoT). Recent work documents that these models can ``self-jailbreak'': without adversarial input modification, the CoT transitions from safety-aware deliberation to committed harmful generation~\cite{harmthoughts,selfjailbreak}. We define the first reasoning step after which safety deliberation permanently ceases as the \textbf{Safety Commitment Point} (CP). This failure mode differs qualitatively from adversarial jailbreaks on standard LLMs because the harmful transition originates within the model's own reasoning. Before building production detectors, a prior question must be answered: can current probing methods reliably distinguish pre-CP from post-CP reasoning steps, and under what conditions? This paper provides a systematic characterization of what hidden-state and text-based probes can and cannot detect.

Existing safety detectors target fundamentally different problems. Hidden-state (HS) methods such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} classify adversarial inputs at the token level, while text monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} scan generated reasoning for explicit violations. Neither tracks the gradual, multi-step commitment process. A practical question is whether a monitoring system should read the model's hidden states or its generated text, but the reliability of HS safety probes depends on methodological choices that have not been systematically examined. Chief among these is layer selection: HS probes require choosing which transformer layer to monitor, a researcher degree of freedom whose metric sensitivity has received almost no scrutiny. We show it can reverse a study's central conclusion.

We present the first systematic evaluation across four reasoning models spanning two architectures (Llama, Qwen) and two scales (7--8B, 32B).
